subject: English
name: English Advanced, Year 12
about: HSC, Human experiences, conversations and craft
syllabus: NSW English Advanced 11-12 Syllabus (2024), Year 12 focus areas

points.title: Individual and collective experience
points.brief: Texts show experiences that belong to one person, such as grief or ambition, and experiences shared by a group, such as war, migration or a community's loss.

points.title: Paradox and contradiction in people
points.brief: People often act against their own stated values or want two things at once. Texts that show these contradictions feel truer, and they invite the reader to question simple judgements.

points.title: Anomalies in behaviour
points.brief: An anomaly is behaviour that breaks a pattern or surprises us, such as an act of kindness from a cruel character. Writers use anomalies to reveal what drives a person.

points.title: Emotions and motivations
points.brief: Texts explore why people act, through fear, love, guilt, pride or hope. Students explain how a writer makes a character's motivation visible to the reader.

points.title: How texts build empathy
points.brief: By placing readers inside an unfamiliar life, through voice, detail and point of view, texts can widen what readers understand of others' experiences.

points.title: Language that conveys experience
points.brief: Precise diction, imagery and rhythm let a writer convey an inner experience, such as anxiety or joy, that is hard to describe directly.

points.title: Shaping a reader's response
points.brief: Writers control what the reader knows and when, and whose view they share, so the reader feels sympathy, suspense or unease at the right moments.

points.title: Writing about experience and the text
points.brief: A strong response links the question's idea of human experience to specific techniques in the text, and explains what the text suggests about people.

points.title: Answering an unseen text question
points.brief: Short-answer questions on unseen extracts ask how a technique shows an experience. Read the question first, find one or two clear examples, and explain the effect in a few sentences.

chapters.title: How texts talk to each other

points.title: Intertextuality
points.brief: Every text draws on earlier texts. Intertextuality is the relationship between texts, through shared stories, characters, forms or ideas, and it shapes how both are read.

points.title: Allusion
points.brief: A brief reference to another text, person or event that the reader is expected to recognise. It adds meaning in a few words.

points.title: Appropriation and transformation
points.brief: A later writer takes an earlier text and reshapes it for a new context, changing its setting, form or point of view. The changes reveal how values have shifted.

points.title: Context and values in paired texts
points.brief: When two texts share a story but come from different times, comparing their contexts explains why they treat the same characters or ideas differently.

points.title: Changing form and medium
points.brief: Moving a story from a play to a film, or a novel to a poem, changes what can be shown and how. Form is part of the conversation between the texts.

points.title: A comparative thesis
points.brief: A thesis for two texts makes one claim about how they relate, such as how the later text challenges the values of the earlier one, rather than two separate claims.

points.title: Integrated paragraphs
points.brief: An integrated essay discusses both texts in each paragraph, around a shared idea. It shows the conversation between texts more clearly than writing on one text and then the other.

points.title: Linking language in comparison
points.brief: Words such as similarly, in contrast, whereas and by reshaping help a reader follow a comparison. They must be followed by explanation, not used alone.

points.title: What the conversation reveals
points.brief: The best comparisons end by explaining what reading the texts together shows that reading either alone would not.

points.title: Style across a whole text
points.brief: A writer's style is the pattern of choices that runs through a text, such as sentence rhythm, imagery or irony. Studying style shows how the whole text makes its meaning.

points.title: Ambiguity and multiple meanings
points.brief: Some texts leave meanings open on purpose, through ambiguous endings, symbols or characters. A strong reading admits the ambiguity and argues for what it adds.

points.title: Critical lenses
points.brief: Readers can approach a text through a lens, such as a feminist, postcolonial, Marxist or psychoanalytic reading, which focuses on power, gender, class or the mind.

points.title: Using critics well
points.brief: Quoting a critic can support or sharpen an argument, but the student's own reading of the text must lead. A critic's view is evidence to test, not a replacement for analysis.

points.title: A personal and informed reading
points.brief: An informed personal response combines close evidence, awareness of context and other readings, and the student's own judgement about what the text achieves.

points.title: A sophisticated thesis
points.brief: A thesis that goes beyond the obvious, by showing tension, change or complexity in the text, such as how its ending complicates what came before.

points.title: Developing an argument across paragraphs
points.brief: Each paragraph should move the argument forward, so the essay builds rather than repeats. Ordering points from simpler to more complex helps.

points.title: Analysing an extract
points.brief: When given a passage from the studied text, connect the details in front of you to the patterns and ideas of the whole text.

points.title: Writing under exam conditions
points.brief: Planning for a few minutes, keeping a clear thesis, and leaving time for a conclusion. A focused argument earns more than covering everything.

points.title: Choosing form and audience
points.brief: Deciding first who the writing is for and what it should do, then picking the form that suits it, such as a short story, speech, personal essay or opinion piece.

points.title: Finding a voice
points.brief: Voice comes from consistent choices in diction, rhythm and attitude. A distinct voice makes writing memorable and persuades a reader to trust the speaker.

points.title: Crafting images
points.brief: A fresh, specific image is stronger than a familiar one. Writers build a central image and return to it so it gathers meaning.

points.title: Structure and pace
points.brief: Paragraph length, scene breaks and the order of events control pace. Slowing down at a moment of tension, or skipping time, shapes how a reader feels.

points.title: Writing dialogue
points.brief: Good dialogue reveals character and moves the story without stating everything. People rarely say exactly what they mean.

points.title: Persuasive writing craft
points.brief: Persuasive pieces use a clear position, evidence, appeals to reason and feeling, and a voice the reader trusts. Rhetorical questions and repetition work best used sparingly.

points.title: Discursive writing craft
points.brief: A discursive piece follows a line of thought, mixes anecdote and reflection, and can change its mind along the way. Its interest lies in the thinking, not a final verdict.

points.title: Reflection statements
points.brief: A reflection explains the choices made in a piece of writing and why, linking them to a studied text or purpose. It discusses craft, not how hard the work was.

points.title: Revising for impact
points.brief: Rereading a draft to cut repetition, sharpen verbs, vary sentence length and check that every part serves the piece's purpose.
